title: SQL vs NoSQL
summary: Select a database around transactions and access patterns, not an unsupported claim that relational storage cannot scale.
body:
Begin with the queries, not the product logo. Are users fetching a document by ID, joining orders to customers, or atomically updating several records? Those access patterns determine the data model and correctness constraints more reliably than predicted traffic.

## Relational versus document and key-value

| Need | PostgreSQL (relational) | Document/key-value store |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cross-entity updates | ACID transactions and foreign keys are natural | Some offer transactions; model and cost vary |
| Related reads | Indexed joins avoid copying shared facts | Denormalize for known read shapes; update every copy |
| Evolving records | Explicit schema and migrations; JSONB where useful | Flexible per-document fields, with validation owned by the application |
| Simple lookup | Indexed row by key | Natural partition-key access, often easy to distribute |

SQL's schema-on-write rejects invalid shapes early; a flexible document model often shifts validation and schema evolution to application reads. This is not “SQL cannot store JSON” or “NoSQL cannot join.” PostgreSQL has JSONB; MongoDB has $lookup and multi-document transactions. But if most reads need several relationships and referential integrity, doing them as joins in SQL is usually simpler than keeping duplicated documents synchronized.

## Transactions and distribution

An order placement might decrement inventory, create an order and record payment state. In PostgreSQL, one transaction can update multiple tables atomically, with constraints enforcing invariants. Some document databases support multi-document transactions too; they are not a free substitute for modeling whether those records live together or across shards. For a known access pattern such as fetching a shopping cart by user ID, a document or DynamoDB item may be a good fit. With denormalization, changing a user's address in three copies needs a reconciliation story.

“Use NoSQL because we will have millions of users” is the wrong shortcut. A well-indexed single PostgreSQL instance may comfortably handle a moderate workload, and read replicas or partitioning are available later. A distributed store adds cross-partition coordination, hot partition keys, capacity planning and different failure behavior. Conversely, a relational schema is not inherently right for high-volume time-series writes or a narrowly keyed global access pattern.

## Design from queries

Write out your hottest read and invariant first. For example, “get the last 20 orders for a user” suggests an index on (user_id, created_at); “charge only once” needs a unique idempotency key and a transactional write. Estimate read and write rates, payload size, consistency requirements and expected growth. Pick a partition key only after checking whether a celebrity account or shared tenant could become hot.

## How to answer this in an interview

> For 100 writes and 1,000 reads per second with orders, customers and inventory, I would start with PostgreSQL and a transactional checkout. I would index (customer_id, created_at) for recent orders. If read latency becomes the bottleneck, I would measure replicas or caching before introducing a second distributed database.
keyTakeaways: Choose from read shapes and invariants rather than assuming NoSQL is inherently faster or SQL cannot scale.
SQL joins and constraints simplify multi-entity consistency; denormalization optimizes known reads but duplicates writes.
Some NoSQL databases support joins and transactions; capability and cross-partition cost vary.
A single indexed PostgreSQL instance is often a better starting point than a distributed store.
